dossier.topic: Warren truss diagonal force sign flip: one equal-length diagonal switches from tension to compression as a load crosses its panel
dossier.summary: A Warren truss is a row of equal-length diagonals and chords that form alternately inverted equilateral triangles. Each diagonal carries axial force only. Under a moving load the sign of a diagonal's force can change, so one bar can be pulled in one load case and pushed in another. Loads on diagonals alternate between compression and tension approaching the centre. The exact load position where a given diagonal flips needs an influence-line calculation.

facts.claim: Loads on the diagonals of a Warren truss alternate between compression and tension, approaching the centre of the span.
The Warren truss is a weight-saving design based on equilateral triangles, forming alternately inverted triangle-shaped spaces along its length.
The Warren truss is named after the British engineer James Warren, who patented it in 1848.
In a Warren truss all panel lengths and diagonals are of equal length, creating a series of equilateral triangles.
Cubitt's Newark Dyke girders connected their members with alternate diagonal struts and ties of cast and wrought iron respectively, on a 240 ft 6 in span.
In the method of joints, any positive member force is tensile and any negative member force is compressive.
The method of joints solves for the unknown forces acting on truss members, and one should start at a joint with only two members connected.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: diagonal sign flip
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Each diagonal of a Warren truss has a force whose sign depends on where the load sits. As a unit load crosses a diagonal's panel the bar goes from one sign to the other, so the same member is pulled in one position and pushed in another.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Draw each diagonal as a bar that is blue when in tension and red when in compression; as a dot load travels the span, bars flip colour one panel behind the load.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: alternating triangle lattice
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Equal-length chords and diagonals form alternately inverted equilateral triangles. Because the diagonals slope in opposite directions from panel to panel, a load on one triangle pushes and pulls its neighbours differently.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Lay out a row of equilateral triangles that point up and down in turn, with bright joints and thin members that brighten when loaded.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: centre-weighted sign zone
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Sources say diagonal forces alternate between compression and tension approaching the centre. Diagonals near midspan therefore carry both signs as the load moves, while end diagonals keep one sign.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Shade a central band of diagonals that pulse between two tones, with end diagonals holding one steady tone.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: cast and wrought split
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Historically the struts were cast iron and the ties were wrought iron, so each sign of force was assigned a different material. The lattice reads as two materials sorted by force sign.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Render struts as thick grey cast forms and ties as thin bright wrought lines; when a diagonal flips sign it changes from one form to the other.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: load-wave sweep
visualisable_mechanisms.description: A moving load sweeps a wave of sign flips across the span over time, so a 20-second piece can build from one flip to a full traverse and settle as the load leaves.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Animate a single load marker crossing left to right over 20 s; flips spread outward from the marker and fade out behind it, with a tone per diagonal that moves up or down in pitch on each flip.

open_questions: At which load position does a given diagonal's force cross zero? This needs an influence-line calculation from a statics text.
Do end diagonals of a Warren truss ever change sign, or only those near midspan? The sources say only that alternation happens approaching the centre.
Does the flip depend on the chord slope, or only on the diagonal's direction in each panel?

surprise.justification: A generalist expects a truss diagonal to be always a brace or always a tie. In a Warren truss the same equal-length diagonal is pulled under one load and pushed under another, and diagonals near midspan carry both signs.

brief.title: Warren truss: the diagonal that flips from pull to push
brief.concept: A mirrored row of equal-length Warren truss diagonals, ochre in tension and rust in compression, flips sign as a load marker crosses each panel.

mechanism_embodied.how_visualised: Each diagonal bar of a mirrored Warren truss is coloured by its solved axial force: ochre when tensile, rust when compressive. A load marker crosses the span over 20 s, and each diagonal changes colour the moment its force crosses zero. The same bar is pulled under one load position and pushed under another, and each flip sounds a tone.

brief.discarded_obvious_idea: Obvious: a truss drawn as grey bars under a moving load, coloured red for hot and blue for cold. Rejected: it is a static diagram with no reason for any force to change, and it hides the sign flip the piece is about.
brief.motion_sound_plan: Mood: high tempo (120 BPM) with a dense field of 60 panels and 120 bars, four hard cuts at 2.5, 7.5, 12.5 and 17.5 s; warm-consonant palette of cream, ochre, rust and graphite with mirrored symmetry; measured framing with one slow pull-back in beat 4; moderate risk, one unfamiliar solver on a safe 2D canvas base. Sound starts on click: a C major triad pulse at 120 BPM, and each sign flip sounds a sine tone, high for tension and low for compression, peak under 0.9. Constraint: none.

storyboard.description: Cream ground, centred wide shot of a mirrored Warren truss of 30 panels, chords and diagonals in graphite. A load marker enters at the left end and the first diagonals take ochre or rust colours from their solved forces.

The marker crosses the left half and diagonals flip from ochre to rust one by one as their force crosses zero. A hard cut at 7.5 s jumps to a close framing of the centre triangles, where bars near midspan show both colours in turn.

The marker reaches midspan and the central diagonals pulse rust and ochre as the load sits near the centre. A thin wave of flips spreads outward from the marker, and a hard cut at 12.5 s tightens the frame on the centre joints.

The marker exits right and the camera pulls back over 5 s to the full mirrored span. Flips fade behind the marker, leaving a settled final pattern of ochre ends and rust centre bars with cream dots on the joints at 20 s.

brief.memorable_moment: A single diagonal turns from ochre to rust at midspan as the marker passes, while the bar beside it stays ochre.
brief.self_declared_risk: Solver sign errors under the moving load, or flips too sparse to read at 2 s. Audio may stutter if a new oscillator is built per flip instead of pooled voices.
brief.liner_note: James Warren patented his truss in 1848. Every panel and diagonal has the same length, and each diagonal carries axial force only. Loads on its diagonals alternate between compression and tension as they approach the centre of the span. In the method of joints a positive member force is tensile and a negative one is compressive, so one bar can be pulled under one load and pushed under another. On screen a load marker crosses a row of equilateral triangles. Each diagonal glows ochre in tension and rust in compression, flipping as its force crosses zero, and each flip sounds a tone.
